title: The Hard Part of Dementia Care Isn't the Dementia Patient, It's the Caregiver Who Gets Dragged Down
dek: The difficulty of dementia care lies not in the patient's condition itself, but in the caregivers who are worn down day after day—care turns wives into nurses and forces post-90s to quit their jobs. Love is the starting point but not the support; the system has yet to catch up with these families.
why: This is not a health guide for the elderly, but a sociologist's honest fieldwork inside dementia-affected families: there are no standard answers, only realities you must see before it's too late.
who: Only children born in the 1980s and 1990s, and urbanites whose parents are aging while they have made no eldercare arrangements; also those who want to understand the real gaps in the care market.

points.h: The care resource gap ultimately falls back on every family
points.body: China has 323 million people aged 60 and above, accounting for 23% of the total population; there are 35 million disabled elderly, yet only about 500,000 eldercare workers. The supply gap is not absorbed by the market or institutions; the pressure mostly falls back on families and individuals. Alzheimer's is not a distant term: reports say China's patient numbers account for nearly 30% of the global total, and the host estimates that on average, one in every 20 Chinese families is affected—for the first generation of only children, this may be the reality their parents are approaching.

points.h: Dementia has no standard symptoms; movies are not to be trusted
points.body: After interviewing 34 families, Tang Yong most wants to correct the misconception that dementia patients have a uniform image. Society's imagination of dementia mostly comes from movies, neighbors, or hearsay; the incontinence of the professor in 'Still Alice' is just one form. He has seen an elderly man who, having been a tailor, still noticed stains on visitors' clothes and taught them to remove them with orange peel; and an elderly woman who, disabled after a car accident, could only hum 'Liuyang River' with focused expression. Dementia itself encompasses Alzheimer's, vascular dementia, and other causes; each person's life imprints remain in different ways, and care cannot follow a script.

points.h: The ideal of a dementia village depends on national care insurance
points.body: Most people see the Dutch dementia village Hogeweyk as the ideal answer: residents live like residents, shopping at the supermarket and going to the café, while staff pose as shopkeepers to maintain a normal atmosphere. But the host adds details that expose how hard it is to replicate: the 23 houses built in 2009 cost over €18 million, of which €17.8 million was borne by the government, and residents' costs are also covered by long-term care-related systems. In contrast, what Tang Yong saw in a low-income U.S. nursing home was the opposite: elevators had to be locked to prevent dementia patients from wandering off. The same disease differs not in philosophy but in the national payment system.

points.h: Love is not enough; sacrifice drags down the caregiver
points.body: The host captures the caregiver's predicament well: many swing between 'I love my parents very much' and 'I'm about to be dragged down by them.' Tang Yong says care is not one-way help but a relationship; when a spouse must learn to bathe, feed, and manage emotions, the original equal partnership is overlaid by a nurse-patient relationship. Long-term sacrifice is not a beautifiable devotion: twenty years ago in Guangzhou, he interviewed a daughter who, after caring for her disabled father, divorced and fell into severe depression; the book also features a post-90s caregiver forced to quit their job due to caregiving pressure. Love is the starting point, but without external resources and community support, caregivers themselves become patients.

points.h: The more you see, the less confident you feel about eldercare
points.body: Having studied eldercare for years, Tang Yong himself has no clear plan for his own parents' care. He is a first-generation only child, and his parents are both 75 this year, but the more cases he sees, the less certain he feels; his research assistant even said after each interview that the more families she saw, the less she knew how to arrange her own parents' future. Multi-child families also have friction: who does more, who pays less, or someone's rough caregiving causes bedsores; only-child families lack shared manpower, and one person who moved their parents to Shenzhen found that rent, medical costs, and nanny fees combined rose faster than retirement wages. An ideal model cannot be designed by a single child independently.

points.h: The pain of dementia care is losing every day
points.body: The biggest difference between dementia care and disability care is that caregivers must repeatedly accept loss. While volunteering in Seattle, Tang Yong observed an elderly man who could initially draw blue lines on wet watercolor paper, but weeks later could only praise others, afraid to put brush to paper; another elderly woman's husband reported new losses every week: his wife couldn't recognize their daughter's newborn grandson, not knowing where this child came from. This daily, irreversible downward slide drains caregivers more than physical disability. The long duration of care is not repetitive hardship but facing a small farewell every day.

points.h: Long-term care insurance has arrived, but it doesn't cover all elderly
points.body: Long-term care insurance was piloted in Qingdao and Shanghai in 2016, and by around 2025 it had expanded to about 90 cities; the official pace is to move toward universal coverage in the next two to three years. But Tang Yong reminds that long-term care insurance does not give money to every elderly person; through unified assessment, it mainly covers those with moderate to severe disability, paying for home care, meal delivery, and other services; those with mild conditions may not qualify. The hardest part is also cultural: sending parents to a nursing home is often equated with filial impiety in China, and elderly people, like the grandfather in the interview, feel their hair would fall out within a month. Tang Yong's judgment is that as younger generations age, the proportion choosing institutional care will rise, but the institutional gap will not disappear automatically.
